gloss: A tank or unit that heats the water used in a building.
examples: The *water heater* is in the garage next to the furnace.
Our *water heater* died after twelve years.
Newer *water heaters* use a lot less gas.

gloss: A machine that cools the air in a room or building.
examples: The *air conditioner* runs all afternoon in July.
We put an *air conditioner* in the bedroom window.
Both *air conditioners* need a new filter.

gloss: The system or process of cooling the air inside a building.
examples: The apartment has *air conditioning* in every room.
The *air conditioning* went out during the heat wave.
I can't sleep without *air conditioning* in August.
contrast: Uncountable — say "the house has air conditioning", never "an air conditioning". The machine itself is an air conditioner.

gloss: The way water is carried away from a place through pipes or ditches.
examples: The yard has terrible *drainage* after a storm.
They dug a trench to improve the *drainage*.
Poor *drainage* is why the basement keeps flooding.

gloss: The waste water and human waste carried away by drains.
examples: Heavy rain pushed raw *sewage* into the river.
The plant treats *sewage* from three towns.
There was a smell of *sewage* in the crawl space.
contrast: Sewage is the waste; a sewer is the pipe that carries it. Don't swap them.

gloss: A mass of material that blocks a pipe or drain.
examples: There's a *clog* somewhere under the kitchen sink.
Hot water and soap cleared the *clog* in a minute.
Hair causes most shower *clogs*.

gloss: A pipe that carries waste water away from a sink, tub, or roof.
examples: The *drainpipe* under the sink was leaking at the joint.
A tree root cracked the old clay *drainpipe*.
Ice split two of the *drainpipes* last winter.

gloss: The force with which water comes out of a pipe or faucet.
examples: The *water pressure* upstairs is really weak.
Something upstream cut our *water pressure* in half.
You need decent *water pressure* for that showerhead.

gloss: The system that brings water to a house, town, or region.
examples: The city shut off the *water supply* for two hours.
The whole *water supply* comes from one reservoir.
Drought put pressure on *water supplies* across the state.

gloss: Water heated for washing, bathing, or cleaning.
examples: We had no *hot water* all weekend.
Run the *hot water* until it gets warm.
The building ran out of *hot water* by seven in the morning.

gloss: Water that comes from a household faucet rather than a bottle.
examples: The *tap water* here tastes like chlorine.
I just drink *tap water* at home.
Is the *tap water* safe in this town?

gloss: Water that is clean enough for people to drink.
examples: The break in the main contaminated the *drinking water*.
They handed out bottled *drinking water* after the flood.
Boil the *drinking water* until the notice is lifted.

gloss: A pipe that carries clean water into or through a building.
examples: A *water pipe* burst behind the wall.
The old *water pipes* in this house are galvanized steel.
They had to open the ceiling to reach the *water pipe*.

gloss: The large public pipe under a street that supplies water to buildings.
examples: A *water main* broke and flooded the intersection.
The city is replacing *water mains* on our block.
Our house is tied into the *water main* at the curb.

gloss: A device that measures how much water a building uses.
examples: The *water meter* is in a box near the sidewalk.
If the *water meter* spins with everything off, you have a leak.
They read the *water meters* once a month.

gloss: The pipe that carries water from the main into a building or fixture.
examples: The plumber ran a new *water line* to the refrigerator.
Shut off the *water line* before you pull the toilet.
Freezing weather cracked one of the *water lines*.

gloss: An underground tank that holds and breaks down household waste water.
examples: The house is on a *septic tank*, not city sewer.
You should pump the *septic tank* every few years.
Two of the *septic tanks* on this road failed inspection.

gloss: A pump in a basement pit that sends collected ground water outside.
examples: The *sump pump* ran all night during the storm.
Get a backup battery for the *sump pump*.
Both *sump pumps* burned out in the same week.

gloss: A unit that moves heat into a building in winter and out of it in summer.
examples: We replaced the old furnace with a *heat pump*.
A *heat pump* struggles a little below freezing.
Rebates brought the price of *heat pumps* way down.

gloss: A small portable heater that warms one room.
examples: I keep a *space heater* under my desk in January.
Never leave a *space heater* running overnight.
The店 sold out of *space heaters* before the cold snap.

gloss: A panel that traps dust as air passes through a heating or cooling system.
examples: Change the *air filter* every three months.
The *air filter* was gray with dust.
I buy *air filters* four at a time.

gloss: An opening that lets air move into or out of a room.
examples: Cold air pours out of the *air vent* by the couch.
Don't put furniture over the *air vent*.
The *air vents* upstairs barely blow anything.

gloss: A metal or fabric tube that carries heated or cooled air through a building.
examples: An *air duct* came loose in the crawl space.
They ran a new *air duct* to the addition.
We had the *air ducts* cleaned before we moved in.

gloss: All the ducts in a building taken together.
examples: Half the *ductwork* in this house is uninsulated.
Replacing the *ductwork* cost more than the furnace.
You can hear the *ductwork* ticking when the heat kicks on.
contrast: Uncountable, like woodwork — say "a lot of ductwork", never "three ductworks".

gloss: A device that adds moisture to dry indoor air.
examples: We run a *humidifier* in the baby's room all winter.
The furnace has a *humidifier* built into it.
Clean your *humidifiers* or they grow mold.

gloss: A machine that pulls moisture out of damp indoor air.
examples: The basement needs a *dehumidifier* in the summer.
I empty the *dehumidifier* every other day.
Two *dehumidifiers* finally dried out the crawl space.

gloss: A fan that pulls stale or damp air out of a room.
examples: Turn on the *exhaust fan* when you shower.
The bathroom *exhaust fan* rattles like a helicopter.
Both *exhaust fans* vent straight through the roof.
contrast: In exhaust the h is silent and the x sounds like /gz/: ig-ZAWST, not eks-HAWST.

gloss: A fan mounted overhead that moves air around a room.
examples: The *ceiling fan* wobbles on the highest setting.
Run the *ceiling fan* in reverse in the winter.
There are *ceiling fans* in all three bedrooms.

gloss: The vented hood above a stove that pulls out smoke and cooking smells.
examples: Turn the *range hood* on before you sear anything.
The *range hood* just recirculates; it doesn't vent outside.
Stainless *range hoods* show every fingerprint.

gloss: The fitting that sprays water down in a shower.
examples: The *showerhead* is clogged with mineral buildup.
I swapped the *showerhead* out in five minutes.
Low-flow *showerheads* save a surprising amount of water.

gloss: The part of a faucet or tap that the water pours out of.
examples: Water dribbles down the outside of the *spout*.
The tub *spout* pulls up to switch to the shower.
These faucets come with taller *spouts*.

gloss: The rounded lower part of a toilet that holds water.
examples: There's a ring of rust in the *toilet bowl*.
The water in the *toilet bowl* drops slowly.
Scrub the *toilet bowls* with something acidic.

gloss: The box behind a toilet that holds the water for each flush.
examples: Lift the lid off the *toilet tank* and look inside.
The *toilet tank* keeps refilling on its own.
Older *toilet tanks* use twice as much water.
contrast: American English calls it a toilet tank; British English calls it a cistern.

gloss: The hinged ring that sits on top of a toilet bowl.
examples: The *toilet seat* is cracked and needs replacing.
Put the *toilet seat* down, please.
Soft-close *toilet seats* are worth the extra ten dollars.

gloss: The basin in a kitchen where dishes are washed.
examples: The *kitchen sink* drains really slowly.
He was standing at the *kitchen sink* peeling potatoes.
Deep *kitchen sinks* are easier to wash pans in.

gloss: The small basin in a bathroom used for washing hands and face.
examples: The *bathroom sink* backs up every morning.
There's a hairline crack in the *bathroom sink*.
Both *bathroom sinks* have the same leaky faucet.

gloss: A grinder under a kitchen sink that chops food scraps so they wash away.
examples: Don't put coffee grounds down the *garbage disposal*.
The *garbage disposal* just hums and won't turn.
Most apartments here have *garbage disposals*.
contrast: The American term; in Britain the same thing is a waste disposal unit.

gloss: A drain set into a floor to carry away spilled or standing water.
examples: The basement has a *floor drain* near the furnace.
Water was backing up out of the *floor drain*.
Commercial kitchens need *floor drains* everywhere.

gloss: The opening in a shower floor that water runs out through.
examples: The *shower drain* is full of hair again.
Water pools around the *shower drain*.
He pulled the covers off both *shower drains*.

gloss: A stopper that closes a drain to hold water in a sink or tub.
examples: Push the *drain plug* down to fill the tub.
The *drain plug* won't seal anymore.
The rubber on these *drain plugs* wears out fast.

gloss: The curved section of drainpipe that holds water and blocks sewer smells.
examples: Put a bucket under the *trap* before you loosen it.
My wedding ring was sitting in the *trap*.
The *traps* dry out in a house nobody lives in.
contrast: Same word as a trap for animals, but in plumbing it means the U-shaped bend under a sink.

gloss: The P-shaped drain trap fitted under a sink.
examples: The *P-trap* under the vanity was full of gunk.
He unscrewed the *P-trap* by hand.
Plastic *P-traps* cost about five dollars.

gloss: Something that stops water or air from moving through a pipe or duct.
examples: The camera found a *blockage* forty feet down the line.
Roots caused the *blockage* in the sewer pipe.
They cleared two *blockages* in one afternoon.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical poured into a drain to dissolve what is blocking it.
examples: I poured *drain cleaner* down the sink and waited.
That *drain cleaner* will eat an old metal pipe.
Most *drain cleaners* are basically lye.

gloss: A long flexible cable pushed into a pipe to break up a clog.
examples: Run the *drain snake* in until you feel resistance.
A twenty-five-foot *drain snake* handles most sinks.
The hardware store rents *drain snakes* by the day.

gloss: A heavy adjustable tool with toothed jaws for gripping and turning pipe.
examples: Grab the big *pipe wrench* out of the truck.
He leaned on the *pipe wrench* until the fitting broke free.
You need two *pipe wrenches* to do this right.
contrast: Americans say wrench where the British say spanner.

gloss: An adjustable wrench with smooth flat jaws.
examples: Tighten the nut with a *monkey wrench*.
The *monkey wrench* is in the bottom of the toolbox.
He owns three *monkey wrenches* and can't find any of them.

gloss: A tool with a small wheel that scores and cuts through pipe.
examples: Use a *pipe cutter* for a clean square end.
The *pipe cutter* won't fit behind the wall.
Small *pipe cutters* work in tight spaces.

gloss: A short connector that joins two pipes or changes their direction.
examples: He needed one more *pipe fitting* to finish the job.
That *pipe fitting* is a half inch too small.
Copper *pipe fittings* have gotten expensive.

gloss: A short sleeve that joins two lengths of pipe end to end.
examples: Slide a *coupling* over the cut and solder it.
The *coupling* started weeping after a month.
Buy a few extra *couplings* while you're there.

gloss: A flat rim on a pipe or fixture that bolts it to something else.
examples: The toilet *flange* is rusted through.
Bolt the *flange* to the floor first.
The *flanges* on these old cast-iron pipes crack easily.

gloss: A T-shaped pipe fitting that splits one line into two.
examples: Put a *tee* here and run a branch to the sink.
The *tee* leaked where the branch came off.
He picked up two *tees* and an elbow.
contrast: Sounds exactly like tea and like the letter T.

gloss: A fitting that connects a wide pipe to a narrower one.
examples: You'll need a *reducer* to go from inch to half inch.
The *reducer* was the wrong size, so nothing lined up.
The bin is full of *reducers* in every size.

gloss: A small rubber ring that seals a joint against leaks.
examples: The faucet dripped until I replaced the *O-ring*.
That *O-ring* is dry and cracked.
A pack of assorted *O-rings* costs almost nothing.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A paste or liquid spread on a joint to keep water or air out.
examples: Run a bead of *sealant* around the base of the tub.
The *sealant* needs a full day to cure.
Silicone *sealants* hold up better in wet rooms.

gloss: The soft flexible material squeezed into seams to seal them.
examples: The *caulking* around the tub is black with mildew.
Scrape out the old *caulking* before you start.
Fresh *caulking* made the whole bathroom look newer.
contrast: The l is silent: KAW-king, not KAWL-king.

gloss: A paste brushed on metal so that solder will flow and stick.
examples: Brush *flux* on both ends before you heat the joint.
Too much *flux* just makes a mess.
Wipe the leftover *flux* off with a rag.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Water pipe made of copper, joined by soldering.
examples: The whole house is plumbed in *copper pipe*.
A length of *copper pipe* costs more every year.
Thieves stripped the *copper pipes* out of the empty building.

gloss: Foam or wrapping put around pipes to keep heat in and frost out.
examples: Slip *pipe insulation* over the lines in the crawl space.
The *pipe insulation* had fallen off years ago.
A few dollars of *pipe insulation* can save a burst pipe.

gloss: Strips of foam or rubber fitted around doors and windows to stop drafts.
examples: New *weatherstripping* cut our heating bill noticeably.
The *weatherstripping* on the back door is shot.
He spent Saturday putting up *weatherstripping*.

gloss: A street drain that carries rainwater away from roads and lots.
examples: Leaves clogged the *storm drain* on the corner.
Everything you pour outside ends up in the *storm drain*.
The city cleaned out the *storm drains* before hurricane season.

gloss: The pipe that carries waste water from a building to the public sewer.
examples: Roots grew into the *sewer line* from the maple out front.
Replacing the *sewer line* meant digging up the yard.
The oldest *sewer lines* in town are made of clay.

gloss: A channel along the edge of a roof that catches rainwater.
examples: The *rain gutter* is packed with pine needles.
Water was pouring over the front *rain gutter*.
We clean the *rain gutters* twice a year.

gloss: The vertical pipe that carries water from a roof gutter to the ground.
examples: The *downspout* dumps water right against the foundation.
Ice pulled the *downspout* off the wall.
Add extensions to the *downspouts* to move water away.
contrast: American downspout is what the British call a drainpipe.

gloss: An outdoor faucet that a hose screws onto.
examples: The *spigot* on the side of the house drips.
Shut the *spigot* off from inside before winter.
There are *spigots* on both ends of the porch.
contrast: A homely American word for an outside tap; the British just say tap.

gloss: The threaded outdoor valve a garden hose attaches to.
examples: The *hose bib* froze and split last January.
He installed a frost-proof *hose bib* out back.
Both *hose bibs* leak at the handle.

gloss: A long flexible tube used to carry water outdoors.
examples: Coil the *garden hose* up before it freezes.
The *garden hose* has a kink near the nozzle.
We keep two *garden hoses*, front and back.

gloss: A network of buried pipes and heads that waters a lawn automatically.
examples: The *sprinkler system* comes on at five in the morning.
We had the *sprinkler system* blown out for the winter.
New houses here all come with *sprinkler systems*.

gloss: A valve that stops the flow of water or gas to a fixture or building.
examples: The main *shutoff valve* is by the water meter.
Every toilet should have its own *shutoff valve*.
The *shutoff valves* under the sink were frozen with corrosion.

gloss: A valve with a quarter-turn handle that opens or closes fully at once.
examples: A *ball valve* is easier to work than an old gate valve.
The handle on the *ball valve* snapped off.
He replaced all the *ball valves* in the basement.

gloss: A valve that lets water flow one way and blocks it coming back.
examples: A *check valve* keeps the sump water from running back in.
The *check valve* is stuck open.
Both *check valves* had to be replaced.

gloss: A valve closed by lowering a flat gate across the pipe.
examples: The old *gate valve* takes ten turns to close.
That *gate valve* has seized up completely.
*Gate valves* were standard in houses built before the seventies.

gloss: A safety valve that opens to release dangerous pressure.
examples: The *relief valve* on the water heater was dripping.
Never cap off a *relief valve*.
Boilers have *relief valves* for exactly this reason.

gloss: A valve that blends hot and cold water to a set temperature.
examples: The shower has a *mixing valve* so the water can't scald you.
The *mixing valve* is set too low.
Modern tubs use thermostatic *mixing valves*.

gloss: The part inside a toilet tank that refills it after a flush.
examples: The *fill valve* keeps running after the tank is full.
A new *fill valve* costs about ten dollars.
He replaced the *fill valves* in both bathrooms.

gloss: The rubber flap at the bottom of a toilet tank that lifts to release water.
examples: A worn *flapper* is why the toilet runs at night.
Drop the new *flapper* over the posts and hook up the chain.
*Flappers* get stiff after a few years.

gloss: A ring of wax that seals a toilet to the drain in the floor.
examples: The leak means the *wax ring* has failed.
Set the toilet down on the *wax ring* in one motion.
Buy two *wax rings* in case you have to reset it.

gloss: A device that removes dirt, taste, or chemicals from water.
examples: The *water filter* on the fridge needs changing.
A *water filter* under the sink handles the whole kitchen.
*Water filters* for that model are hard to find.

gloss: A unit that removes the minerals that make water hard.
examples: We put in a *water softener* and the spots on the glasses stopped.
The *water softener* needs a bag of salt every month.
*Water softeners* are almost standard around here.
contrast: The t in soften is silent: SAW-fuh-nur.

gloss: Water with a lot of dissolved minerals, which leaves deposits.
examples: *Hard water* leaves white spots on everything.
The whole county has *hard water*.
*Hard water* shortens the life of a water heater.

gloss: A cooling system that serves a whole house through ducts.
examples: The house has *central air*, which is rare on this street.
We finally put in *central air* last summer.
Without *central air*, August is rough.
contrast: Everyday American short form of central air conditioning; uncountable.

gloss: An air conditioner that sits in a window opening.
examples: We run a *window unit* in the bedroom.
The *window unit* drips onto the sidewalk.
He hauled the *window units* up from the basement in May.

gloss: All the equipment that warms a building.
examples: The *heating system* in this building is sixty years old.
Get the *heating system* serviced before October.
Older *heating systems* waste a lot of fuel.

gloss: A long low heater that runs along the bottom of a wall.
examples: Don't push the couch against the *baseboard heater*.
The *baseboard heater* clicks as it warms up.
Electric *baseboard heaters* are expensive to run.

gloss: Heating that warms a room from pipes or wires in the floor.
examples: The bathroom has *radiant heat* under the tile.
*Radiant heat* is slow to come up but very even.
They put *radiant heat* in the whole first floor.

gloss: Heating in which a boiler sends steam through pipes to radiators.
examples: The building still runs on *steam heat*.
*Steam heat* makes those banging noises in the pipes.
You can't control *steam heat* room by room.

gloss: The part of a furnace or boiler that passes heat from burning fuel to air or water.
examples: A cracked *heat exchanger* means the furnace has to be replaced.
The technician looked at the *heat exchanger* with a camera.
*Heat exchangers* usually last about twenty years.

gloss: The indoor unit that blows heated or cooled air into the ducts.
examples: The *air handler* is up in the attic.
Water was pooling under the *air handler*.
Large buildings have several *air handlers*.

gloss: The fan inside a furnace or air handler that pushes air through the ducts.
examples: The *blower* runs but no heat comes out.
A bad bearing made the *blower* squeal.
Variable-speed *blowers* are much quieter.

gloss: A movable plate inside a duct or flue that controls how much air passes.
examples: Close the *damper* when the fireplace isn't in use.
Somebody shut the *damper* in the upstairs duct.
The *dampers* are adjusted twice a year.

gloss: The grille in a floor or wall where heated or cooled air enters a room.
examples: Warm air comes up through the *register* by the window.
Vacuum the dust out of the *register*.
The rug is covering two of the *registers*.
contrast: Not the cash register or a school register — in a house it is the heating vent's grille.

gloss: A ceiling or wall fitting that spreads incoming air evenly around a room.
examples: Cold air blows straight down out of that *diffuser*.
They angled the *diffuser* away from the desks.
The office has *diffusers* every ten feet.

gloss: One of a set of angled slats that let air through an opening.
examples: Rain never gets past the *louver* on the vent.
Dust had caked on every *louver*.
The attic *louvers* keep the roof space cool.
contrast: American spelling louver; British spelling louvre.

gloss: The replaceable filter that cleans air on its way into a furnace.
examples: I forgot to change the *furnace filter* all winter.
A dirty *furnace filter* makes the system work harder.
*Furnace filters* come in a dozen sizes.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The fluid that carries heat out of a cooling system.
examples: The unit was low on *refrigerant*.
A technician has to be licensed to handle *refrigerant*.
Newer *refrigerants* are less harmful to the ozone layer.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid circulated through a system to carry heat away.
examples: The loop was almost out of *coolant*.
*Coolant* leaked onto the floor of the mechanical room.
Different *coolants* freeze at different temperatures.

gloss: The indoor coil where refrigerant absorbs heat from the air.
examples: Ice formed on the *evaporator* and airflow stopped.
The *evaporator* sits right above the furnace.
Dirty *evaporators* cut cooling capacity in half.

gloss: The water that forms when warm moist air cools on a cold surface.
examples: The *condensate* drains into a small pump.
*Condensate* was backing up and spilling over.
A clogged line let *condensate* run down the wall.

gloss: A shallow tray that catches water dripping from a unit.
examples: The *drip pan* under the air handler was full.
Put a *drip pan* under the water heater.
Rusted-through *drip pans* cause a lot of ceiling damage.

gloss: A small sensor that shuts off the gas if the pilot flame goes out.
examples: A bad *thermocouple* is why the pilot won't stay lit.
The *thermocouple* costs almost nothing to replace.
*Thermocouples* wear out every few years.

gloss: The pipe that brings natural gas or propane to an appliance.
examples: They ran a *gas line* to the new stove.
Never dig without checking where the *gas line* is.
All the *gas lines* have to be pressure tested.

gloss: The valve that controls gas flowing into a furnace or water heater.
examples: Turn the *gas valve* to the off position.
The *gas valve* failed and the furnace wouldn't fire.
*Gas valves* on these units are sealed at the factory.

gloss: The device outside a building that measures how much gas it uses.
examples: The *gas meter* is on the side of the house.
Somebody came out to read the *gas meter*.
The *gas meters* for all six units are in one row.

gloss: Gas escaping from a pipe or fitting where it should not.
examples: If you smell a *gas leak*, get out and call from outside.
The crew traced the *gas leak* to a loose fitting.
Two *gas leaks* were reported on the same street.

gloss: An alarm that sounds when dangerous levels of carbon monoxide build up.
examples: Every floor should have a *carbon monoxide detector*.
The *carbon monoxide detector* went off at two in the morning.
Test your *carbon monoxide detectors* twice a year.

gloss: A tank holding the fuel oil that a furnace burns.
examples: The *oil tank* is down to a quarter.
An old *oil tank* in the basement can leak.
Buried *oil tanks* are a headache when you sell a house.

gloss: A small tank that takes up the extra volume of water as it heats.
examples: Code requires an *expansion tank* on the water heater.
The *expansion tank* had lost its air charge.
*Expansion tanks* hang off the cold water line.

gloss: A small pump that moves hot water through a heating loop.
examples: The *circulator* hums whenever the heat is on.
A seized *circulator* left the upstairs cold.
The boiler feeds three *circulators*, one per zone.

gloss: The room in a building that holds the boiler and heating equipment.
examples: The super keeps his tools in the *boiler room*.
It's a hundred degrees in the *boiler room*.
*Boiler rooms* have to be kept clear of storage.

ru: подсобное помещение (с котлом и стиральной машиной)
gloss: A small room that holds the furnace, water heater, and laundry machines.
examples: The water heater is in the *utility room* off the kitchen.
There's a floor drain in the *utility room*.
The newer units all have *utility rooms*.

gloss: The low space under a floor where pipes and ducts run.
examples: The pipes in the *crawl space* aren't insulated.
He crawled under the house to look at the *crawl space*.
Damp *crawl spaces* lead to mold upstairs.

gloss: The movement of air through a system or room.
examples: A dirty filter kills *airflow*.
There's almost no *airflow* from the vent in the back room.
They redesigned the ducts to improve *airflow*.

gloss: How clean and healthy the air in a place is.
examples: Better ventilation improved the *air quality* in the classroom.
The *air quality* indoors is worse than people think.
Smoke from the fires ruined the *air quality* for a week.

gloss: An opening or pipe that carries away water when a basin gets too full.
examples: Water runs out the *overflow* before the sink can spill.
The *overflow* on the tub was plugged with soap.
Both sinks have *overflows* near the rim.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, OH-vur-floh; the verb is oh-vur-FLOH.

gloss: Water flowing backward into a clean supply line.
examples: The valve is there to prevent *backflow*.
*Backflow* can push dirty water into the drinking supply.
The city tests for *backflow* every year.

gloss: A tube that draws liquid up and over a rim by suction.
examples: He used a *siphon* to empty the flooded pit.
Start the *siphon* by filling the hose first.
Simple *siphons* work with no pump at all.
contrast: The ph sounds like f, and the word is also spelled syphon.

gloss: The banging in pipes when flowing water is stopped suddenly.
examples: You hear *water hammer* every time the washer shuts off.
*Water hammer* can eventually crack a joint.
An arrestor on the line cured the *water hammer*.

gloss: A pipe that has split open, usually from freezing or pressure.
examples: A *burst pipe* flooded the whole first floor.
The insurance covered the damage from the *burst pipe*.
Cold snaps mean a week of *burst pipes* for plumbers.

gloss: A pipe blocked by ice because the water inside it froze.
examples: Nothing came out of the faucet — a *frozen pipe*.
Thaw a *frozen pipe* slowly with a hair dryer.
Leave a faucet dripping and you avoid most *frozen pipes*.

ru: повреждения от воды, ущерб от протечки
gloss: Harm done to a building by leaking or standing water.
examples: There's *water damage* on the ceiling under the bathroom.
The leak caused thousands of dollars of *water damage*.
They repainted to hide the *water damage*.
contrast: Damage is uncountable — say "a lot of water damage", never "water damages".

gloss: Water covering an area that is normally dry.
examples: The broken main caused *flooding* in three basements.
*Flooding* in the crawl space rusted out the ducts.
We get *flooding* down here every spring.

gloss: A small amount of liquid falling one drop at a time.
examples: That *drip* kept me awake half the night.
A slow *drip* wastes gallons a week.
There were *drips* forming along the joint.

gloss: A vertical pipe that carries water or steam up through a building.
examples: The *riser* runs up through all six floors.
They shut down the *riser* to fix the leak.
The old *risers* are being replaced one line at a time.

gloss: A capped opening in a drain line that lets a plumber reach a clog.
examples: The *cleanout* is buried somewhere in the front yard.
He pulled the cap off the *cleanout* and ran the snake in.
Newer houses have *cleanouts* at every turn in the line.

gloss: A pipe that lets air into a drain system so water flows and smells escape.
examples: A blocked *vent pipe* makes the drains gurgle.
The *vent pipe* comes out through the roof.
Birds had nested in one of the *vent pipes*.

gloss: The short flexible tube that feeds water to a fixture.
examples: The *supply line* to the toilet let go overnight.
Use a braided *supply line*, not the plastic kind.
Replace the *supply lines* whenever you change a faucet.

gloss: An open space in a drain line that keeps dirty water from being sucked back.
examples: The dishwasher drains through an *air gap* on the counter.
Water sprayed out of the *air gap* when the drain clogged.
Some codes require *air gaps* on every appliance drain.

gloss: The bad-smelling gas that rises out of drains and sewers.
examples: A dry trap lets *sewer gas* into the room.
The basement smelled of *sewer gas* for weeks.
*Sewer gas* is not just unpleasant; it can be dangerous.

gloss: The heavy round lid over an opening into a sewer or utility shaft.
examples: Steam was rising through the *manhole cover*.
A truck knocked the *manhole cover* loose.
The city stamps the year onto its *manhole covers*.

gloss: A pit under a street grate that collects runoff and traps debris.
examples: The *catch basin* on the corner is full of silt.
Crews vacuum out the *catch basin* every spring.
Blocked *catch basins* flood the whole intersection.

gloss: A metal frame of bars covering a drain or opening.
examples: My keys went through the *grate* into the storm drain.
Leaves were piled against the *grate*.
The *grates* are bolted down so nobody steals them.
contrast: Sounds exactly like great.

gloss: A large pipe that carries a stream or runoff under a road or driveway.
examples: The *culvert* under the driveway is crushed.
Water backed up because the *culvert* was plugged.
The county replaced two *culverts* on this road.

gloss: A tank for storing water, often rainwater.
examples: The farmhouse collects roof water in a *cistern*.
The *cistern* holds about two thousand gallons.
Old stone *cisterns* still sit under some of these yards.
contrast: In American English a cistern is a water storage tank; in British English it usually means a toilet tank.

gloss: The pump that brings water up out of a private well.
examples: The *well pump* burned out and we had no water for a day.
A new *well pump* runs a couple thousand dollars.
Deep wells need submersible *well pumps*.

gloss: A machine that moves water through pipes.
examples: The *water pump* kicks on whenever someone runs a faucet.
They hooked a portable *water pump* to a hose.
Two *water pumps* keep the building supplied.

gloss: A private waste water system with a tank and a buried drain field.
examples: The inspector wants to look at the *septic system*.
Grease is hard on a *septic system*.
*Septic systems* out here have to be permitted.

gloss: The buried lines of perforated pipe that let treated waste water soak into the soil.
examples: Don't park a truck over the *drain field*.
The grass above the *drain field* is greener than the rest.
Failed *drain fields* are expensive to replace.

gloss: The thick solid material that settles out of waste water.
examples: *Sludge* had built up on the bottom of the tank.
The plant dries the *sludge* before hauling it away.
Black *sludge* was coming out of the pipe.

gloss: Liquid waste that flows out of a tank, plant, or building.
examples: The *effluent* leaves the tank and soaks into the field.
They test the *effluent* before it reaches the creek.
Treated *effluent* is used to water the golf course.

ru: серые стоки (вода из раковин и душа)
gloss: Used water from sinks, showers, and washing machines, but not toilets.
examples: They reuse *graywater* on the garden.
*Graywater* has to be kept separate from the sewer line.
A *graywater* system needs a permit in this county.
contrast: American spelling graywater; British writing uses greywater.

gloss: A device that removes contaminants from water or air.
examples: We keep a water *purifier* on the counter.
The *purifier* takes out most of the chlorine taste.
Air *purifiers* sold out during the fire season.

gloss: A facility that cleans water before it is piped to homes.
examples: The *water treatment plant* sits down by the river.
A power failure shut the *water treatment plant* down.
Two *water treatment plants* serve the whole county.

gloss: Water that is safe to drink.
examples: The sign says the tap is not *potable water*.
The campground has one *potable water* station.
Every unit must have a *potable water* supply.
contrast: Say POH-tuh-bul, not PAH-tuh-bul; it has nothing to do with pot.

gloss: A deep plain sink used for dirty jobs, usually in a basement or garage.
examples: Rinse the brushes in the *utility sink*.
The *utility sink* drains into the same line as the washer.
Plastic *utility sinks* are cheap and hard to break.

gloss: A washbasin, or the small room containing one.
examples: The plans call for a *lavatory* in the powder room.
The *lavatory* at the back of the plane was occupied.
Both *lavatories* need new faucets.
contrast: In American plumbing catalogs a lavatory is the bathroom sink itself; in everyday speech it mostly survives on airplanes.

gloss: A wall-mounted fixture in a men's restroom.
examples: The *urinal* on the end is out of order.
They installed a waterless *urinal*.
All four *urinals* flush automatically.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, YUR-uh-nul; the British say yoo-RY-nul.

gloss: A low bathroom fixture, or a seat attachment, used for washing after the toilet.
examples: The hotel bathroom had a *bidet* next to the toilet.
He installed a *bidet* attachment on the toilet seat.
*Bidets* are far more common in Europe than in the States.
contrast: From French: the final t is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable, bih-DAY.

gloss: Any sink, tub, toilet, or shower connected to the water and drain lines.
examples: Every *plumbing fixture* in the house is original.
The permit covers moving one *plumbing fixture*.
They picked out all the *plumbing fixtures* before framing started.
contrast: The b in plumbing is silent: PLUM-ing.

gloss: A coiled tool cranked into a drain or toilet to clear a blockage.
examples: A toilet *auger* got the clog out in a minute.
Feed the *auger* in slowly and keep turning.
Plumbers carry several *augers* of different lengths.
contrast: Sounds the same as augur, meaning to foretell.

gloss: A water heater that warms water only as it flows, with no storage tank.
examples: A *tankless water heater* never runs out of hot water.
The *tankless water heater* needs a bigger gas line.
*Tankless water heaters* cost more up front.

gloss: A heater that burns compressed wood pellets fed in automatically.
examples: The *pellet stove* heats the whole downstairs.
We go through a ton of pellets a winter in that *pellet stove*.
*Pellet stoves* need electricity to run the auger.

gloss: A person whose job is cleaning soot out of chimneys and flues.
examples: We have a *chimney sweep* come every fall.
The *chimney sweep* found a crack in the liner.
Good *chimney sweeps* book up before winter.
